The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

derivations.claim: The product is a Hilbert space: if a sequence is Cauchy in the finite sum-of-squares norm, each edge coordinate is Cauchy in its $H^1$ norm and converges by [F1]; the finitely many coordinate limits form an element of the product and the sum of the finitely many squared errors tends to zero. The product inner product is the sum of the edge inner products.

For each edge $e$, choose $\epsilon_e=\ell_e/2$, which satisfies the hypothesis of [F2]. For either endpoint, [F2] then gives  $$\max\{|w_e(0)|^2,|w_e(\ell_e)|^2\}\le\frac{4}{\ell_e}\|w_e\|_{L^2(0,\ell_e)}^2+\ell_e\|w'_e\|_{L^2(0,\ell_e)}^2\le C_e\|w_e\|_{H^1(0,\ell_e)}^2,$$  where $C_e:=\max\{4/\ell_e,\ell_e\}<\infty$. Thus each endpoint evaluation is a bounded linear functional on its edge $H^1$ space. For every vertex, the difference of two incident endpoint evaluations is therefore continuous; its kernel is closed. Each anchor endpoint evaluation is also continuous and its zero set is closed. There are finitely many vertices, incidences, and anchors, so the intersection of these kernels, namely the trace-matching space and then $V_D$, is closed in the product.

A Cauchy sequence in either constrained space converges in the product by step 1.1. Continuity of every endpoint functional from step 1.2 passes all matching equalities and zero anchor values to the limit, so the limit remains in the same constrained space. The restricted edge-product inner product is positive definite and complete there. Hence both constrained spaces are Hilbert.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: If $E=\varnothing$, then $H=\{0\}$ and the inequality is $0\le0$. Otherwise fix an edge $e$ in a component containing an anchor. If $e$ is a loop, deleting its interior leaves the component connected because any path that traverses the loop can omit that closed excursion. If its endpoints are distinct, every original path that uses $e$ reaches one endpoint before traversing it; after deleting $e$, vertices are therefore connected to one of its two endpoints. Thus removing $e$ either leaves the component connected or separates it into two components, one containing each endpoint. In the connected case choose either endpoint; in the separated case choose the endpoint in the component containing an anchor. By [F3] there is a finite path from an anchor to that endpoint avoiding $e$. Deleting the portions between repeated vertices gives a simple path, so no edge is traversed twice. For a loop choose its tail incidence; otherwise use the incidence at the chosen endpoint. For any $x$ on $e$, append the segment from that incidence to $x$. The total length is at most $L_\Gamma$, and the common vertex traces agree along the path by [F1]. Since $w=0$ at the anchor, [F1] and [F2] imply $$|w_e(x)|^2\le L_\Gamma \sum_{a\text{ on the concatenated path}}\int_a|w'_a|^2 \le L_\Gamma\sum_{a\in E}\|w'_a\|_{L^2(a)}^2.$$

Integrate the pointwise bound of step 1.1 over every edge and sum. The total measure of the disjoint edge interiors is $\sum_e\ell_e=L_\Gamma$, so $$\|w\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}^2\le L_\Gamma^2\sum_{e\in E}\|w'_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2.$$ Taking nonnegative square roots proves the statement.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

By [F1] and [F4], $u'_e$ and $v_e$ have absolutely continuous representatives on $[0,\ell_e]$. They are bounded there. Applying [F2] to the product therefore yields $$\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e =-\int_0^{\ell_e}u''_ev_e\,dx_e +u'_e(\ell_e)v_e(\ell_e)-u'_e(0)v_e(0).$$ The endpoint terms are the head and tail outward derivatives paired with their traces.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with ordered vertices
$V=\{v_i:i<n\}=\{v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\}$ and ordered edges
$E=\{e_j:j<m\}=\{e_0,\dots,e_{m-1}\}$. Choose, for each edge
$e_j=\{u,w\}$, one endpoint as its tail and the other as its head. The resulting
$n\times m$ matrix $B=(b_{ij})$ with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$ is an **oriented
incidence matrix** of $G$, where, for $i<n$ and $j<m$,

$$b_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }v_i\text{ is the head of }e_j,\\-1,&\text{if }v_i\text{ is the tail of }e_j,\\0,&\text{if }v_i\notin e_j.\end{cases}$$

Each column therefore has exactly one $1$ and one $-1$, because every edge of a
simple graph has exactly two distinct endpoints. Different choices of

$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.

axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: The canonical inclusion $i:V_D\to H$ is continuous because $\|v\|_H\le\|v\|_{V_D}$. It is injective because $V_D$ consists of Sobolev classes included in the edge-product $L^2$ classes. To prove density, fix $g=(g_e)\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. By [F2] and finite choice, choose for each of the finitely many edges a $\phi_e\in C_c^\infty(0,\ell_e)$ with $\|g_e-\phi_e\|_{L^2(e)}<\epsilon/\sqrt{|E|}$. The edge-product function $\phi=(\phi_e)$ has zero endpoint traces, hence belongs to $V_D$, and $\|g-\phi\|_H^2=\sum_e\|g_e-\phi_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2<\epsilon^2$. Thus the range of i is dense in H.

By [F1] and [F3], H and V_D are real Hilbert spaces with dense continuous inclusion. With V_D^* as its continuous real dual, these spaces form the evolution triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The mesh has finitely many cells, and a P1 function is determined by its finite list of nodal values; the vertex matching and anchor conditions are linear. Therefore V_h is a finite-dimensional subspace of V_D by [F8].

By [F4] and [F6], the form a is bounded by M=κmax and coercive by α on V_D, hence also on V_h. The restriction F_h(t):=f(t)|_{V_h} is a bounded functional and its norm is at most \|f(t)\|_{V^*}; restriction is a continuous linear map from V_D^* to V_h^*, so F_h is strongly measurable and square-integrable. Thus all hypotheses of [F5] hold for the evolution triple and finite P1 subspace of step 1.2.
Applying [F5] gives the unique semidiscrete solution and its energy estimate for every t in [0,T]. No spatial approximation rate is part of [F5], so none follows here.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

By [F2], $$\|v\|_{V_D}^2=\|v\|_H^2+\|v'\|_H^2\le(1+L_\Gamma^2)\|v'\|_H^2.$$ Consequently $$a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\min}\|v'\|_H^2\ge\frac{\kappa_{\min}}{1+L_\Gamma^2}\|v\|_{V_D}^2.$$ The form is coercive with $\alpha=\kappa_{\min}/(1+L_\Gamma^2)>0$.

Fix an edge and take $v$ smooth with compact support in its interior and zero on every other edge. The vertex sum vanishes, so the integral of $-\kappa_eu''_e-f_e$ against every such test is zero. This residual is in $L^2(0,\ell_e)$; density from [F7] and continuity of the pairing by [F5] imply $-\kappa_eu''_e=f_e$ almost everywhere on that edge. Now fix a free vertex $z$. Both incidences of a loop at $z$ receive value $1$, so this defines a trace-matching test function in $V_D$. Substitution in step 2.1 and the interior equation just proved leaves only the flux sum at $z$, so it is zero. This proves the stated natural Kirchhoff condition.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with ordered vertex and edge sets.
Choose an orientation of each edge and let $B\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}$ be
the resulting incidence matrix of
[[def-oriented-incidence-matrix-of-a-graph]]: a column has $-1$ at its tail,
$+1$ at its head, and zero elsewhere. Let $D\subseteq V$ be the vertices with
prescribed Dirichlet values and let $I=V\setminus D$ be the free vertices.
Assign a mass $m_i>0$ to each $i\in I$ and a conductance $c_e\ge0$ to each
$e\in E$. Put

$$M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)_{i\in I},\qquad C=\operatorname{diag}(c_e)_{e\in E},\qquad L_C=BCB^{\mathsf T}.$$

The matrix $L_C$ is the **conductance-weighted graph stiffness**. Its free
Dirichlet restriction $L_D$ is the principal submatrix $(L_C)_{I,I}$. The
finite weighted network diffusion equation is

$$M u'(t)+L_Du(t)=f(t),$$

where $u(t)\in\mathbb R^I$ and $f(t)\in\mathbb R^I$. If $D=\varnothing$,
this is the closed Neumann network equation. If the boundary values are
instead a nonzero vector $g(t)$, restriction of $L_C(u,g)$ to $I$ gives
$M u'+L_Du=f-(L_C)_{I,D}g$.

When every $c_e=1$, $L_C=BB^{\mathsf T}$ agrees with the ordinary graph
Laplacian by
[[thm-laplacian-is-the-oriented-incidence-product]]. Zero conductances are
allowed and remove those edges from the diffusion coupling; they do not remove
the vertices or masses.

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

derivations.claim: If $I=\varnothing$, all free-state assertions are vacuous, so assume $I\ne\varnothing$. Put $Q=-LM^{-1}$. For distinct free vertices $i,j$, $Q_{ij}=-L_{ij}/m_j\ge0$ by [F1]. If $D=\varnothing$, [F1] says that $\mathbf1$ is constant on every positive-conductance component, so $L\mathbf1=0$; symmetry gives $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L=0$. Thus $Q$ has zero column sums and is a finite column generator by [F2]. If $p_0\ge0$ is nonzero, let $s=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}p_0>0$ and $\pi=p_0/s$. By [F2], $e^{tQ}\pi$ is a probability vector, so it is entrywise nonnegative; multiplying by $s$ proves $e^{tQ}p_0\ge0$. If $p_0=0$, its image is zero.

If $D\ne\varnothing$, then $Q$ has nonnegative off-diagonal entries and diagonal entries $Q_{ii}=-L_{ii}/m_i$. Put $\lambda=\max_{i\in I}L_{ii}/m_i\ge0$. If $\lambda=0$, then $L_{ii}=\sum_{e\text{ incident to }i}c_e=0$ for every free vertex. Since each $c_e\ge0$, every conductance incident to a free vertex is zero; hence each free row of $L_D$ vanishes, $Q=0$, and its exponential is the identity. If $\lambda>0$, every entry of $Q+\lambda I$ is nonnegative. For $t\ge0$, each term of the matrix series $e^{t(Q+\lambda I)}=\sum_{k\ge0}t^k(Q+\lambda I)^k/k!$ is entrywise nonnegative. By [F3], since $-\lambda tI$ commutes with $t(Q+\lambda I)$, $$e^{tQ}=e^{-\lambda tI}e^{t(Q+\lambda I)}=e^{-\lambda t}e^{t(Q+\lambda I)}$$ is entrywise nonnegative.

The diagonal entries of $E_F(\tau)$ are $1-\tau L_{ii}/m_i$, and its off-diagonal entries are $-\tau L_{ij}/m_i\ge0$ by [F1]. Thus all entries are nonnegative exactly when each diagonal is nonnegative, which is exactly $\tau\le m_i/L_{ii}$ for every $i$ with $L_{ii}>0$. If a diagonal is negative, applying the step matrix to the corresponding coordinate vector produces a negative coordinate, so the condition is sharp.

The mass state $p=Mu$ satisfies $p'=Qp$ for the homogeneous network equation. Its solution is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p(0)$. Since $M$ and $M^{-1}$ are entrywise positive diagonal matrices, $$u(t)=M^{-1}e^{tQ}Mu(0)=e^{-tM^{-1}L}u(0),$$ where the second equality follows term by term from the matrix exponential series applied to the similarity $M^{-1}QM=-M^{-1}L$. Steps 1.1–1.2 therefore prove positivity of $S_D(t)$ for both boundary cases.

Let $y\ge0$ and solve $(M+\tau L)x=My$. The matrix is symmetric positive definite because for nonzero $x$, $x^{\mathsf T}(M+\tau L)x\ge\sum_i m_i x_i^2>0$ by [F1]; hence the solve exists uniquely. If $x_k<0$ is a minimum coordinate, extend $x$ by zero on $D$. The edge formula for $(Lx)_k$ is a sum of terms $c_e(x_k-\bar x_{\mathrm{other}(e)})$, each nonpositive because every free neighbor has value at least $x_k$ and every Dirichlet value is zero. Therefore $((M+\tau L)x)_k=m_kx_k+\tau(Lx)_k<0$, contradicting $(My)_k=m_ky_k\ge0$. Thus $x\ge0$ and backward Euler is positivity preserving.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite metric graph and anchor set $D$, the trace-matching space and
the anchored space $V_D$ of
[[def-anchored-finite-metric-graph-h1-space]] are closed real Hilbert
subspaces of $\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R)$ with the
edge-product $H^1$ inner product.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the hypotheses and notation of
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and
suppose additionally that $a$ is Hermitian:
$a(v,w)=\overline{a(w,v)}$. Then
$$\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$$
is the energy norm and the Galerkin solution is its best approximation:
$$\|u-u_h\|_a=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_a.$$

[[def-anchored-finite-metric-graph-h1-space]], a mesh
$\mathcal T_h$ of [[def-metric-graph-p1-edge-mesh]], positive constants
$\kappa_e$ on the edges, and edgewise $u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$ as in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], with the
trace matching and anchor conditions of $V_D$. Let $I_hu$ be the edgewise
nodal linear interpolant. Then $I_hu\in V_h$ and

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Orient each edge coordinate from $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ to $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For endpoint incidences
$(e,-)$ and $(e,+)$ define the outward derivatives by
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,-)}}u_e=-u'_e(0)$ and
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,+)}}u_e=+u'_e(\ell_e)$. The two incidences are both
included at a loop vertex. For $\iota=(e,\pm)$ write $e(\iota)=e$.
If $u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$, with $H^2$ as defined by
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]],
$v\in V_D$, and each edge has a constant diffusivity $\kappa_e>0$, then

$$\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e =-\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u''_ev_e\,dx_e +\sum_{z\in V}v(z)\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z).$$

Thus zero test traces remove anchored endpoint terms, and a Kirchhoff
condition
$\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z)=0$ at each free vertex
cancels the remaining terms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, $E\ne\varnothing$, and that the anchor set $D$ meets every connected
edge component of the finite metric graph $\Gamma$. Let constant edge
diffusivities satisfy
$$0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_e\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty.$$
For every $f\in H=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R)$ there is a unique
$u\in V_D$ such that

$$a(u,v):=\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e=F(v):=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}f_ev_e\,dx_e\qquad(v\in V_D).$$

The equation is the anchored weak metric-graph diffusion problem. Whenever
$u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$ as defined in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], the Green identity
[[lem-metric-graph-kirchhoff-green-identity]] identifies its interior
equation as $-\kappa_eu''_e=f_e$ and its natural free-vertex condition as
Kirchhoff balance of the outward diffusive fluxes.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and assume every connected edge component of the finite metric graph $\Gamma$
has at least one anchor in $D$. Put
$L_\Gamma=\sum_{e\in E}\ell_e$. Then every $w\in V_D$ satisfies

$$\|w\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}\le L_\Gamma \left(\sum_{e\in E}\|w'_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

At a directed network junction, let $n_{\rm in}$ edges carry nonnegative
incoming **mass fluxes** $q^{\rm in}_i$ into the junction, and let
$n_{\rm out}$ edges carry outgoing mass fluxes. A **conservative nonnegative

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with ordered vertex and edge sets.
Choose an orientation of each edge and let $B\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}$ be
the resulting incidence matrix of
[[def-oriented-incidence-matrix-of-a-graph]]: a column has $-1$ at its tail,
$+1$ at its head, and zero elsewhere. Let $D\subseteq V$ be the vertices with
prescribed Dirichlet values and let $I=V\setminus D$ be the free vertices.
Assign a mass $m_i>0$ to each $i\in I$ and a conductance $c_e\ge0$ to each
$e\in E$. Put

$$M=\operatorname{diag}(m_i)_{i\in I},\qquad C=\operatorname{diag}(c_e)_{e\in E},\qquad L_C=BCB^{\mathsf T}.$$

The matrix $L_C$ is the **conductance-weighted graph stiffness**. Its free
Dirichlet restriction $L_D$ is the principal submatrix $(L_C)_{I,I}$. The
finite weighted network diffusion equation is

$$M u'(t)+L_Du(t)=f(t),$$

where $u(t)\in\mathbb R^I$ and $f(t)\in\mathbb R^I$. If $D=\varnothing$,
this is the closed Neumann network equation. If the boundary values are
instead a nonzero vector $g(t)$, restriction of $L_C(u,g)$ to $I$ gives
$M u'+L_Du=f-(L_C)_{I,D}g$.

When every $c_e=1$, $L_C=BB^{\mathsf T}$ agrees with the ordinary graph
Laplacian by
[[thm-laplacian-is-the-oriented-incidence-product]]. Zero conductances are
allowed and remove those edges from the diffusion coupling; they do not remove
the vertices or masses.

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

The vector $(1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ has dot product $1$ with the first component indicator, while every vector in the image of the symmetric matrix $L_C$ is orthogonal to its kernel: for $z=L_Cx$ and $k\in\ker L_C$, $k^{\mathsf T}z=(L_Ck)^{\mathsf T}x=0$. Thus this load is not in the image and the Neumann steady equation has no solution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the cited one-dimensional
representative interface. A **finite metric graph**
$\Gamma=(V,E,\partial_-,\partial_+,\ell)$ consists of finite vertex and
edge sets $V,E$, endpoint maps $\partial_-,\partial_+:E\to V$, and edge
lengths $0<\ell_e<\infty$. Distinct edges with the same endpoints are
allowed, as are loop edges with $\partial_-e=\partial_+e$. Every vertex is
an endpoint of at least one edge. The two endpoint incidences $(e,-)$ and
$(e,+)$ remain distinct even for a loop. A graph path is a finite sequence
$z_0,e_1,z_1,\ldots,e_n,z_n$ with $n\ge0$ and
$\{\partial_-e_j,\partial_+e_j\}=
\{z_{j-1},z_j\}$ for every $j$; a loop permits $z_{j-1}=z_j$. Vertices in
the same connected edge component are those joined by such a path. Orient
each edge only to choose its coordinate $x_e\in[0,\ell_e]$, with $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ and $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For $z\in V$, let
$\mathcal I(z):=\{(e,-):\partial_-e=z\}\cup\{(e,+):\partial_+e=z\}$
be its finite set of endpoint incidences.
The edge-product spaces are

$$H:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}L^2(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R),\qquad \mathcal W:=\bigoplus_{e\in E}H^1(0,\ell_e;\mathbb R).$$

For $w_e\in H^1(0,\ell_e)$, its endpoint values mean the values of the unique
absolutely continuous representative supplied by
[[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].
The **trace-matching graph Sobolev space** is the subspace of $\mathcal W$
whose endpoint-incidence traces all agree at each vertex. For a designated
anchor set $D\subseteq V$, define the **anchored graph energy space**

$$V_D:=\{w\in\mathcal W:\ w_{\iota}=w_{\iota'}\text{ whenever }\iota,\iota'\in\mathcal I(v),\quad w_{\iota}=0\text{ for each }v\in D,\ \iota\in\mathcal I(v)\}.$$

We equip $H$ with the edge-sum $L^2$ inner product and $V_D$ with

$$\|w\|_{V_D}^2=\sum_{e\in E}\int_0^{\ell_e}(|w_e|^2+|w'_e|^2)\,dx_e.$$

No Kirchhoff derivative condition is built into $V_D$; that condition is a
natural boundary condition of the later weak diffusion form. The elliptic
and P1 error results below assume that $D$ meets every connected edge
component.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Orient each edge coordinate from $0$ at
$\partial_-e$ to $\ell_e$ at $\partial_+e$. For endpoint incidences
$(e,-)$ and $(e,+)$ define the outward derivatives by
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,-)}}u_e=-u'_e(0)$ and
$\partial_{\nu_{(e,+)}}u_e=+u'_e(\ell_e)$. The two incidences are both
included at a loop vertex. For $\iota=(e,\pm)$ write $e(\iota)=e$.
If $u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$, with $H^2$ as defined by
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]],
$v\in V_D$, and each edge has a constant diffusivity $\kappa_e>0$, then

$$\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u'_ev'_e\,dx_e =-\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\int_0^{\ell_e}u''_ev_e\,dx_e +\sum_{z\in V}v(z)\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z).$$

Thus zero test traces remove anchored endpoint terms, and a Kirchhoff
condition
$\sum_{\iota\in\mathcal I(z)}\kappa_{e(\iota)}\partial_{\nu_\iota}u_{e(\iota)}(z)=0$ at each free vertex
cancels the remaining terms.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

The outward derivative at the tail $x=0$ is $-u'_i(0)$. The three values are $-1,+1,0$, whose sum is $0$. Each edge has $u_i''=0$. Therefore the edge equation has zero load and the free central vertex satisfies Kirchhoff balance.
